headline_marked: GitHub Octoverse 2026: [[AI agents draft 40%+ of GitHub PRs]], up from 17% in March
headline: GitHub Octoverse 2026: AI agents draft 40%+ of GitHub PRs, up from 17% in March
summary: GitHub's latest Octoverse report reveals a surge in AI agent-assisted development, with over 110 million agent-started pull requests in September alone. These PRs also merge faster, with 90% completing within two weeks.
details: GitHub's Octoverse 2026 report highlights a significant shift in code contribution. By September 2026, over 40% of all pull requests on GitHub were initiated with a first draft from a coding agent, a substantial increase from 17% in March of the same year. This translates to 110 million agent-started PRs in a single month.

GitHub defines "agent-started" PRs as those where the initial draft was detected as coming from an AI agent. This metric counts pull requests, not lines of code, and represents a floor, meaning the actual involvement of AI could be even higher.

The velocity of agent-involved PRs is noteworthy; 90% merged within two weeks in September, compared to approximately 86% for non-agent-involved PRs. Agents also tend to touch more files, with 87% being multi-file compared to 79% for human-started PRs.

The report covers October 2025 to September 2026, noting 1.3 billion merged PRs and 34.3 billion commits. Furthermore, 55% of Copilot monthly users now utilize agentic features, up from 35% a year prior.

TypeScript, Python, and JavaScript are the top languages for agent-assisted development. The report also indicates that 61% of users who select models use more than one, with no single model holding more than a 25% market share.

The key takeaway for developers is a shift in the bottleneck from writing code to reviewing it. Teams that effectively review agent output are expected to thrive, as the 40% figure is a growing trend.

headline_marked: [[Cloudflare's AI served customer data to others]] due to GPU memory mismatch on Workers AI
headline: Cloudflare's AI served customer data to others due to GPU memory mismatch on Workers AI
summary: Between August 27 and September 9, 155 responses from Cloudflare's GLM-5.3 model on Workers AI contained fragments of other customers' requests, specifically for prompts longer than 681,280 tokens.
details: Cloudflare's Workers AI experienced a data exposure incident between August 27 and September 9. During this period, 155 responses from the GLM-5.3 model inadvertently included fragments of data from other customer requests.
The issue specifically affected prompts longer than 681,280 tokens. No external hacking occurred; the incident stemmed from an internal bug involving GPU memory allocation.

The root cause involved two concurrent problems. First, the GLM-5.3 model advertised a ~1M-token context window, but the GPUs' KV cache pool could only fit 681,280 tokens. The SGLang system, which computes this pool from leftover GPU memory, failed to verify it against the advertised length.

Second, when an over-length prompt arrived, SGLang's disaggregated prefill/decode path marked it as rejected but did not abort processing. Consequently, the decode node generated responses using stale cache pages that held data from previous requests.

Cloudflare's response was swift and transparent. After a researcher reported the issue via HackerOne on September 8, Cloudflare reproduced it within 25 minutes on September 9, pulled the model within 40 minutes, and rolled out a fix to all nodes, restoring service the same evening.

The company then collaborated with SGLang maintainers on upstream fixes (v0.5.21+). They published a full postmortem detailing their errors, emphasizing the importance of verifying actual GPU memory against advertised context lengths.

Customers who sent prompts longer than 681,280 tokens to GLM-5.3 during the affected window (Aug 27–Sep 9) are advised to contact Cloudflare support. Users self-hosting SGLang with disaggregated serving should upgrade to versions past v0.5.22 to mitigate similar risks.
